posts.name: Douglas Porter
posts.content: A quick note to set the record straight, since my Oct 19 line is making the rounds. I did say September CPI "did nothing to advance the case for interest rate hikes", and I stand by it: ex-gasoline 2.2% (from 2.4%), CPI-trim 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9%. But I did not say the Bank will hold at 2.25%. BMO's published call is a 25 bp hike to 2.50% on Wednesday. Both can be true. One soft month of core inflation doesn't outweigh oil at US$113-117 (vs. the ~US$75 the Bank assumed in July), its September warning about upside risks, and a business survey where half of firms plan to pass on costs. BoC preview (Oct 28): BMO Economics expects a 25 bp hike to 2.50% from 2.25%. It's a close call. The latest Reuters poll split 19-15.

• Headline CPI was 3.1% y/y in September, up for a second month
• Brent is ~US$113-117, compared with the ~US$75 assumed in the July MPR
• The Bank warned in September that upside inflation risks had increased
• In the Bank's Oct surveys, about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter aren't sure when inflation returns to 2%

Why it could be a hold:
• CPI ex-gasoline eased to 2.2%, and core measures were soft. As Douglas Porter noted, the September report did nothing to advance the hike case on its own
• Growth is soft, at ~1.9% in Q3 and ~1.3% in Q4, with 50% US tariffs weighing

What to watch: the new MPR oil assumption and forward guidance. A hawkish hold would keep December in play. We'll post our reaction after the 9:45 a.m. ET decision. Full reasoning is in this week's Focus.

What we're weighing:
• September CPI was 3.1% y/y, up from 3.0% in August and just below the 3.2% consensus.
• BoC surveys show about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases. Nearly a quarter can't say when inflation will return to 2%. That's an unanchoring risk.
• Growth is slowing. Monthly GDP was flat in July, and the flash estimate for August shows 0.2%. The new US tariffs are weighing on Q4.

As CIBC's Andrew Grantham noted, the data give policymakers time. We continue to expect the first hike in January 2027, and the risks are tilted toward it coming earlier if price pressures persist. The loonie firmed from 1.4097 to 1.3993 per USD between Oct. 19 and Oct. 23, consistent with markets pricing a less dovish outlook.

Several forecasters now expect a 25 bp hike next week. Differing views are a normal part of forecasting. On Wednesday we'll be watching the statement's language on inflation expectations and cost pass-through, and the MPR's updated growth and energy assumptions.

This post is for general information only and isn't investment advice.

posts.content:
Bank of Canada preview, Oct. 28 | Our view: we expect the Bank to hold at 2.25%.

Key takeaways:
• Underlying inflation is near target. September CPI-median eased to 1.9% from 2.0%, CPI-trim is at 1.8%, and CPI excluding gasoline slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%. Headline CPI of 3.1% mostly reflects gasoline, which was up 27.8% y/y.

In our view, a supply-driven oil shock hitting a slowing, tariff-exposed economy doesn't yet make a convincing case for tightening.

What this means for Canadian businesses: the forward guidance may matter more than the decision itself. Watch the statement's language on inflation expectations, the energy assumptions in the MPR and the tone at the 10:30 a.m. ET press conference. Exporters and borrowers should plan for several rate and tariff scenarios rather than bet on one outcome.

Our economics team, including Peter Shannon, will post a reaction right after the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement.

posts.name: RBC
posts.content:
BoC preview, Oct 28 – RBC Economics: we continue to expect the Bank of Canada to hold its policy rate at 2.25%.

The Reuters poll (Oct 21–23) now has 19 of 34 economists calling for a 25 bp hike, and peers including BMO have set out a careful case for one. We take that case seriously. Our reasons for still calling a hold:

• Underlying inflation is easing. September headline CPI was 3.1% y/y, but most of that came from gasoline (+27.8% y/y). Excluding gasoline, CPI slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%, and CPI-trim (1.8%) and CPI-median (1.9%) are both below 2%.
• Growth is weak. Reuters-polled economists see growth slowing from ~1.9% in Q3 to ~1.3% in Q4, before the full effect of the 50% US tariffs on roughly US$20B of Canadian goods.
• The Canadian dollar firmed from 1.4097 to 1.3993 per USD between Oct 19 and Oct 23. That eases some imported inflation pressure, but it also adds to the strain on exporters already hit by tariffs.

Risks are tilted toward a firmer tone. Brent near US$113–117 is well above the Bank's July assumption of ~US$75. About half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter can't say when inflation will return to 2%. The ECB raised rates in June and September.

What would change our view: a broadening of price pressures into core and services, a further rise in inflation expectations, or an MPR that sharply raises its oil assumption and flags pass-through as the main concern.

On Wednesday, the guidance matters more than the decision itself. We'll react to the 9:45 a.m. ET statement and MPR, and to the 10:30 press conference. Read our full analysis on RBC Economics.

This is a forecast, not investment advice.

posts.name: Sherry Cooper
posts.content:
Bank of Canada preview for Oct 28. My call: the Bank of Canada will hold rates steady at 2.25%. This is a closer call than any decision in more than a year, and the market consensus has shifted. The latest Reuters poll has 19 of 34 economists expecting a 25 bp hike, and BMO and Desjardins have both switched to hike calls. I respect those views. The upside risk to inflation is real. Brent is above US$113, compared with the US$75 the Bank assumed in July. About half of firms plan to pass on cost increases. Macklem warned on Oct 17 that the risk of inflation broadening has increased, and the Fed hiked in September.

Why I still expect a hold:
• The data do not support a hike yet. CPI excluding gasoline eased to 2.2% from 2.4%, and the core measures (CPI-trim and CPI-median) softened.
• Growth is stalling. July GDP was flat, Q4 is tracking around 1.3%, and the Governor himself says it could fall below 1% if the 50% US tariffs stay.
• An oil supply shock is better looked through than fought. A hike won't lower the price of crude, and it would hit an economy already suffering from tariffs. That would be a policy error unless inflation expectations clearly de-anchor.
• There is also little room to cut while inflation risks are rising.

What to watch at 9:45 a.m. ET and the 10:30 press conference:
• Language on inflation expectations and cost pass-through.
• The MPR's revised oil and growth assumptions.
• Whether the forward guidance explicitly opens the door to a December or January move.

My base case is a hawkish hold. If the Bank hikes, I'll own it and update my analysis.

Takeaways for borrowers:
• Variable rates: payments would stay the same on a hold, but budget now for a possible 25 to 50 bp of tightening by early 2027.
• Fixed rates: pricing follows the 5-year GoC yield, which has already moved up on hike expectations.
• Renewing in the next 4 months? Lock in a rate hold now. It costs nothing and protects you if yields keep rising.

Stay tuned. I'll post live coverage Wednesday morning.

posts.name: Economists surveyed
posts.content:
Reuters poll summary: Bank of Canada decision, 28 October 2026 (34 economists polled 21–23 October 2026)

Distribution of calls: 19 of 34 expect a 25 bp hike to 2.50% from 2.25%. 15 do not forecast a hike. That's a slim majority for tightening and a large minority against it. The split itself tells us something: the profession thinks this decision is unusually close.

Hawkish arguments (reported data):
• September CPI was 3.1% y/y, up from 3.0% (StatCan, 19 Oct)
• In BoC surveys released 19 Oct, consumers' long-term inflation expectations rose, about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter can't say when inflation will return to 2%. That's a de-anchoring risk.
• Oil is well above the July MPR assumption

Hold arguments (reported data):
• CPI excluding gasoline eased to 2.2% from 2.4%. On 19 Oct, BMO's Douglas Porter said the CPI report did nothing to advance the case for hikes.
• LFS (9 Oct): employment fell 68k in September after falling 42k in August. Unemployment rose to 6.5% and wages were up 2.3% y/y.
• 50% US tariffs on about US$20B of Canadian goods have been in place since talks broke down on 21 Aug
• Continuum Economics expected a hold as of 21 Oct

Poll GDP estimates (forecasts, not data): about 1.9% in Q3 and 1.3% in Q4 2026.

Context: the last hike was in July 2023, to 5.00%. A long easing cycle then brought the rate to 2.25% by 29 Oct 2025. A hike now would reverse that direction.

What to watch: the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement, the MPR's oil and growth assumptions, and the 10:30 a.m. ET press conference with Governor Macklem and SDG Rogers. Guidance for December may matter more than the 25 bp.

Polls show what economists expect, not what will happen. We'll report afterward whether the majority or the minority got it right. This is not investment or mortgage advice.

posts.name: Standard Chartered
posts.content:
Bank of Canada preview (28 October 2026): We keep the call we published on 20 October. Our base case is that the Bank holds the overnight rate target at 2.25%, where it has been since 29 October 2025, and pairs the hold with cautious-to-hawkish guidance.

The Reuters poll of 21-23 October has 19 of 34 economists expecting a 25bp hike to 2.50%, so we are in the minority. We take that shift seriously. On balance, though, we think the data still support patience.

Why we expect a hold:
- Headline CPI was 3.1% y/y in September, but most of that came from gasoline (+27.8% y/y). Excluding gasoline, CPI eased to 2.2% from 2.4%.
- Growth is slowing. Consensus is about 1.9% in Q3 and about 1.3% in Q4, as the 50% US tariffs on roughly US$20bn of Canadian goods, in place since talks broke down on 21 August, weigh on activity.

Why risks are skewed to a hike:
- Brent settled at US$113.17 on 22 October and traded near US$117 on 23 October. The July MPR assumed roughly US$75.
- In the Bank's 19 October surveys, about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter cannot say when inflation will return to 2%. That suggests expectations may be drifting.
- The Bank said on 2 September that upside risks to inflation had increased, and on 21 September that it did not want to be too slow to respond.

What we will watch: the new MPR oil assumption and 2027 inflation path, how the Bank assesses tariff damage to growth, and the signals from Governor Macklem and Senior Deputy Governor Rogers at the 10:30 a.m. ET press conference.

What would change our view: a clear move higher in inflation expectations, firmer core trim and median, or MPR projections that push the return to 2% beyond the forecast horizon. A hawkish hold would keep 9 December live.

Our reaction will follow the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement, including implications for CAD and Canadian rates. If the Bank hikes, we will say so and update our forecasts.

For informational purposes only. This does not constitute investment advice.

posts.content:
Ahead of the Bank of Canada decision on Oct. 28, here is what it could mean for your borrowing and savings.

• Variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit: these follow prime, which moves with the Bank's policy rate. If the Bank holds at 2.25%, prime stays where it is. A 25 bp hike would usually flow through to prime soon after.
• Fixed-rate mortgages: these are priced mainly off bond yields, which already reflect what markets expect. Fixed rates can move before or after a decision, not only on the day itself.
• Savings: higher-rate expectations can support yields on GICs and high-interest savings. Rates differ by product and term.
• Businesses facing tariffs and higher input costs: plan for several scenarios, both rates and tariffs. Review cash flow, credit facilities and supplier exposure now.

Our view is still a hold on Oct. 28, with risks tilted toward an earlier hike if price pressures persist. Either way, we suggest planning for a range of outcomes rather than betting on one.

Have questions about your own situation? Please talk to a CIBC advisor or reach us through our secure client channels. Please don't share account details here.

Bank of Canada Preview: What Wednesday Means for Your Mortgage

Headline: The Bank's policy rate has been 2.25% since October 29, 2025. The decision comes Wednesday, Oct 28, at 9:45 a.m. ET, together with a new Monetary Policy Report. Governor Macklem and SDG Rogers hold their press conference at 10:30 a.m.

The latest Reuters poll leans 19-15 toward a 25 bp hike, mostly because of Brent near US$113-117 and business surveys showing firms plan to pass on costs. Here's why we still expect a hold:
• CPI excluding gasoline eased to 2.2%, and the core measures are soft
• The 50% US tariffs are weighing on growth. The Reuters poll has Q4 near 1.3%
• Raising rates won't bring down the price of oil, and it would add strain for indebted households

🔹 Fixed-rate shoppers and renewals: fixed rates track the five-year Government of Canada bond yield, not Wednesday's decision directly. If you're renewing in the next 120 days, ask about a rate hold.
🔹 First-time buyers: you still have to qualify under the stress test, so get pre-approved before rates move.

We'll post a same-day reaction at 9:45 and cover the 10:30 tone, hawkish or dovish. Every situation is different, so talk to a DLC mortgage expert about yours.

BoC Oct 28 rate question: forecast tally and resolution reminder (as of Sat 24 Oct)

1. Status quo: 2.25% target, unchanged since 29 Oct 2025. Decision at 9:45 a.m. ET Wed 28 Oct, with the MPR. Press conference ~10:30 a.m. ET.

2. Published calls I've reviewed (9-23 Oct):
   - Hike 25bp to 2.50%: BMO, Desjardins, Scotiabank
   - Hold at 2.25%: TD, CIBC (first hike Jan 2027), RBC (as of 19 Oct), KPMG, Continuum, plus the hold previews posted here
   - Cut: none. Reuters poll 21-23 Oct: 19 of 34 hike, 15 hold, 0 cut.

3. The disagreement comes down to one issue: whether to act on leading indicators (half of firms planning pass-through, rising long-term consumer expectations, Brent ~US$113-117 vs ~US$75 assumed in July) or lagging ones (CPI-trim 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9%, ex-gas 2.2%). Both readings are reasonable.

5. A reminder, because I'll get asked on Wednesday: a 'hawkish hold' resolves 'no change.' Guidance doesn't count, only the rate does. Exactly 2.25% after the announcement = no change. Anything else = change, rounded per the published rules. Emergency moves outside the scheduled announcement don't count.

Read the resolution criteria now. Edge cases are where questions go to die.

Global Week Ahead | Bank of Canada, Wed. Oct. 28 (9:45 a.m. ET decision, 10:30 a.m. ET press conference)

Our call: a 25 bp hike to 2.50%. As Derek Holt said on Oct. 19, it's not a slam dunk, but there is probably enough evidence to support one.

Why we can't just look through the oil shock:
• Looking through a supply shock works when expectations are anchored. The Bank's Oct. 19 surveys suggest they may not be. About half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, nearly a quarter can't say when inflation returns to 2%, and consumers' long-term expectations rose.
• Brent at US$113–117 is roughly US$38 above the July MPR assumption of ~US$75.
• The Bank flagged higher upside risks in September and said it did not want to be "too slow."

What could prove us wrong:
• CPI excluding gasoline is 2.2% and easing, and trim and median are below 2%.
• Employment fell by about 110k over August and September.
• 50% US tariffs on ~US$20B of goods could cut Q4 growth below 1%.

How we'll read each outcome:
• Hike: the key is whether guidance frames it as insurance or the start of a cycle. 16 of 29 in the Reuters poll see another hike by end-March 2027.
• Hold: if the MPR raises its oil assumption and pushes the return to 2% later, Dec. 9 is live.

CAD: the move to 1.3993 from 1.4097 (Oct. 19–23) partly reflects markets repricing the odds of a hike. A hold could reverse some of that.

What this means for borrowers: variable rates follow prime. Fixed rates follow GoC yields, which already price in some tightening.

Reaction thread within minutes of 9:45. If we're wrong, we'll explain why and what it means for the path ahead. Read the full note at Scotiabank Economics.

Views are those of Scotiabank Economics and subject to revision. This is not investment advice.

posts.name: Peter Shannon
posts.content:
KPMG Canada | BoC preview, Oct 28: what it means for business

Our call: we expect the Bank to hold at 2.25%. It's a close call. The Reuters poll is 19-15 in favour of a 25 bp hike, and we take the opposing case seriously.

Why we expect a hold:
• Underlying inflation is easing. CPI ex-gasoline fell to 2.2% from 2.4%, and trim (1.8%) and median (1.9%) are below 2%. The 3.1% headline is mostly an energy story, with gasoline up 27.8% y/y.
• Demand is weakening. Employment fell in both August and September, unemployment is at 6.5%, and Q4 GDP is tracking ~1.3%, possibly below 1% if the 50% US tariffs stay.
• A hike won't lower the price of a barrel of Brent. It would add pressure on firms already absorbing tariff costs.

Why risks are tilted toward a hike:
• Brent at ~US$113-117, about US$38 above the July MPR assumption
• About half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter can't say when inflation returns to 2%
• The Fed hiked in September, widening the rate gap with the US

What we'll be watching on Wednesday: the MPR's new oil and growth assumptions, the projected date for inflation returning to 2%, and whether Macklem and Rogers describe the energy shock as a one-time level shift or as persistent inflation. We expect a hawkish hold that keeps a December or January hike in play.

For businesses, the takeaway is:
1. Budget for higher borrowing costs into 2027 whatever happens Wednesday.
2. Stress-test margins in two scenarios: oil staying above US$110, and the tariffs persisting.
3. Review cost-pass-through plans against softer demand. Customers may push back harder than surveys suggest.
4. Tariff-exposed firms should look at the federal support channels (work-sharing, BDC/EDC liquidity).

If the Bank hikes, we'll say so and update our outlook. Our post-decision analysis for clients will follow the 10:30 a.m. ET press conference.

Views are forecasts, not investment advice.

posts.content:
The assumption versus the reality: our Bank of Canada preview for Oct. 28

When the Bank published its July MPR, it assumed Brent at about US$75. On Oct. 22 Brent settled at US$113.17, and Reuters had it near US$117 the next day. That gap of roughly US$38 a barrel runs through everything the October MPR has to update: the inflation path, Canada's terms of trade and the growth outlook.

Here's what has changed since July:
• Aug. 21: Canada-US trade talks broke down, and 50% US tariffs on about US$20B of Canadian goods followed
• Sept. 16: the Fed hiked to 3.75–4.00%. The Bank has been at 2.25% since Oct. 29, 2025
• Sept. CPI (StatCan): 3.1% y/y headline, 2.2% ex-gasoline (down from 2.4%), with gasoline up 27.8%
• Oct. 19 BoC surveys: about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter can't say when inflation returns to 2%
• Reuters poll (Oct. 21–23): 19 of 34 economists expect a 25 bp hike and 15 don't. GDP forecasts are about 1.9% in Q3 and 1.3% in Q4

The forecasters are split. BMO and Desjardins call a hike. TD and CIBC expect a hold, with the first move by January 2027 at the latest. Continuum Economics also expects a hold.

The dilemma: Monetary policy usually looks through a supply shock. But that only works if inflation expectations stay anchored, and the Bank's own surveys suggest they are starting to slip. A hike into a tariff slowdown carries risk. So does a hold that the market reads as tolerating 3% inflation.

What to watch on Wednesday:
1. The MPR's new oil assumption, and how candidly it explains the miss from July
2. When the Bank now expects inflation to return to 2%
3. Whether the statement treats energy as a one-time level shift or as a broadening pressure
4. Guidance for December and early 2027 from Governor Macklem and SDG Rogers at 10:30 a.m. ET

We won't guess the call. We'll have coverage from 9:45 a.m. ET, then follow up with the summary of deliberations and the Nov. 6 jobs report.

Disagree with how we've framed this? Send us a counter-argument or an op-ed pitch.

posts.name: Economists polled by Reuters
posts.content:
BoC Oct. 28: what counts as a surprise either way. Reuters poll: 34 economists, surveyed Oct. 21–23.

• Hike to 2.50%: 19 of 34 (slim majority)
• Hold at 2.25%: 15 of 34 (sizeable minority)
• Cut: none
• 16 of 29 expect at least one more hike by end-March 2027

With the panel split this closely, neither outcome is a non-event. A hike would surprise about 44% of the panel. A hold would surprise about 56%.

From public previews, the hike camp includes BMO, Desjardins and Scotiabank. The hold camp includes TD, CIBC, KPMG, RBC (as of Oct. 19) and Continuum Economics. Each firm's view is its own.

Several forecasters on both sides say the gap between a "hawkish hold" and a "dovish hike" is smaller than the headline split suggests. Context from public sources that will shape how the decision is read:
– The MPR's new oil assumption. July assumed ~US$75 Brent. Brent settled at US$113.17 on Oct. 22.
– Revisions to growth. Poll medians are ~1.9% for Q3 and ~1.3% for Q4. Macklem says Q4 growth could fall below 1% if the 50% US tariffs stay.
– Whether the projected return to 2% inflation moves later.
– Forward guidance, and how the 10:30 a.m. ET press conference describes pass-through.

After the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement we'll post the result against the poll. Next major data point: the Nov. 6 jobs report.

This is a poll summary, not a guarantee or investment advice.

posts.name: Continuum Economics
posts.content:
BoC preview, Oct 28: our scenarios

Our base case, published 21 Oct, is still a hold at 2.25%. The decision is close, so here is how we weigh the outcomes:

• Hawkish hold, ~55%: Rate unchanged. The MPR raises the inflation path and lowers growth, and the guidance clearly keeps a December or January move open.
• 25 bp hike to 2.50%, ~40%: Framed as insurance against second-round effects, followed by a signal of a long pause rather than the start of a new cycle.
• Dovish hold, ~5%: Rate unchanged with the emphasis on tariff-driven weakness. We think this is unlikely given the Bank's September warning on upside risks.

Why we lean toward a hold:
• Underlying inflation is soft. CPI-trim is 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9% and CPI ex-gasoline 2.2%. The 3.1% headline rate is mostly energy.
• Slack is building in the labour market. Employment fell about 110k across Aug–Sep, unemployment is 6.5% and wage growth is 2.3% y/y.
• Growth is uneven. Q2 grew 3.3% annualized, July was flat and the August flash was 0.2%. Q4 could fall below 1% if the 50% US tariffs stay.

Upside risks we take seriously: Brent at ~US$113–117 against the ~US$75 July assumption, about half of firms planning to pass on costs, rising long-term consumer expectations, and global tightening (Fed, ECB).

What would move us to the hike camp: a materially lower potential-growth estimate in the MPR, a projected return to 2% pushed beyond the horizon, or statement language that treats expectations as de-anchoring.

We'll publish a rapid review after the 9:45 a.m. ET decision and the 10:30 press conference. If we get it wrong, we'll say so and explain why.

This is research commentary, not investment advice.

posts.name: Reuters
posts.content:
EXPLAINER: Five things to watch in the Bank of Canada's Oct. 28 decision

1. The rate: The policy rate has been 2.25% since Oct. 29, 2025. Economists polled by Reuters Oct. 21-23 are split 19-15 in favour of a 25 bps hike to 2.50%; none forecast a cut.

2. The oil assumption: The July MPR assumed Brent at about $75 a barrel. Brent settled at $113.17 on Oct. 22. Economists say the revised assumption and the projected date for inflation to return to 2% will be closely watched.

3. Inflation measures: September headline CPI rose 3.1% y/y, with gasoline up 27.8%. CPI excluding gasoline eased to 2.2% from 2.4%; CPI-trim was 1.8% and CPI-median 1.9%, below the 2% target.

4. Labour market and growth: Employment fell by 42,000 in August and 68,000 in September, and the unemployment rate is 6.5%, according to figures cited by economists. Reuters-polled economists see GDP growth slowing to about 1.3% in Q4 from 1.9% in Q3. Governor Tiff Macklem has said Q4 growth could fall below 1% if the 50% US tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian goods remain.

5. Expectations and guidance: In the Bank's October business surveys, about half of firms planned to pass on cost increases. Macklem said on Oct. 17 the risk of inflation broadening had increased. Several forecasters expecting a hold say a firmer tone in guidance could keep the Dec. 9 meeting in play.

Decision and MPR at 9:45 a.m. ET; press conference at about 10:30 a.m. ET. Reuters will carry live coverage.

posts.name: Leslie Preston
posts.content:
What we'll be watching in Wednesday's Bank of Canada decision (9:45 a.m. ET) and Monetary Policy Report:

1. The call. We continue to expect a hold at 2.25%. Headline CPI is 3.1% y/y, but excluding gasoline it eased to 2.2% in September. That isn't the broad-based acceleration in underlying inflation that would justify a hike.
2. The oil assumption. In July the Bank assumed about US$75 for oil. Brent settled at US$113 on Oct 22. How the Bank treats that gap, as a temporary shock or a persistent one, will shape the inflation path.
3. Language on broadening. Look for whether the warning from Oct 17, that the risk of inflation broadening has increased, becomes explicit guidance that rates are biased toward tightening.
4. Tariffs and growth. The Governor has said the 50% US tariffs could cut Q4 growth to below 1%. How much weight does the MPR give to that slack?
5. Expectations. Business surveys show about half of firms planning to pass on costs. Second-round effects are the key risk to monitor.

Base case: a hawkish hold that keeps 2027 tightening in play. Risks are tilted toward an earlier move, and the 19-15 Reuters poll split shows how close this call is. If the Bank hikes, we'll say so promptly and update our outlook. Our full reaction will follow the release. This is a forecast, not advice.

posts.name: Reuters
posts.content:
US says 50% tariffs on Canadian goods remain in place; Ottawa calls them unjustified

The United States said on Saturday its 50% tariffs on about US$20 billion of Canadian goods, in effect since trade talks broke down on Aug. 21, remain in place. In a statement, Washington said the tariffs respond to "Canada's unwillingness to agree to fair and reciprocal terms" and that "the door to negotiations remains open." It said it respects central bank independence and would not comment on Bank of Canada decisions. The statement attributed rising energy prices to Iran.

The Government of Canada said in response that it has negotiated in good faith and "will not accept a bad deal just to get a deal." It called the tariffs unjustified and contrary to the spirit of CUSMA/USMCA, and said its response would be "firm, proportionate and strategic."

The exchange comes four days before the Bank of Canada's Oct. 28 rate decision. Governor Tiff Macklem has said Q4 growth could fall below 1% if the tariffs remain. Economists polled by Reuters Oct. 21-23 are split 19-15 in favour of a 25 bps hike to 2.50%.

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content: Respectfully, I read it differently. Stripping out gasoline doesn't make the oil shock go away. Energy costs show up in transport, food and services prices with a lag, and that's the second-round effect the Bank can't ignore. Look at the Bank's own surveys too: about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter can't say when inflation gets back to 2%. That points to expectations starting to come unanchored. Brent around US$113-117 against a July assumption of ~US$75, plus 50% US tariffs on roughly US$20B of Canadian goods, means more cost pressure is coming. Growth is softening (we estimate ~1.9% in Q3 and ~1.3% in Q4), and I accept that this is a close call. It's not a slam dunk. But on balance of risks, 25bp on Oct 28 is the better risk management. What matters is where core and expectations go from here, not one month of ex-gas CPI.

comments.name: Reuters
comments.content: Clarification on the Reuters poll: of 34 economists polled Oct. 21-23, 19 forecast a 25 bps hike to 2.50% on Oct. 28; the remaining 15 expect no change. The majority view reverses the previous poll's consensus for a hold. 16 of 29 respondents expect another hike by end-March 2027. Growth forecasts: about 1.9% in Q3, 1.3% in Q4. Full story and methodology on reuters.com.

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content: "Preventing higher energy prices from feeding into broader inflation" is the right goal, but it's hard to square with waiting until the pass-through is already here. Your own surveys show about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases and nearly a quarter can't say when inflation returns to 2%. Those are leading indicators, and core is the lagging one. Yes, tariffs could cut Q4 growth to below 1%, and I don't dismiss that drag. But a weaker CAD and Brent at US$113+ against a ~US$75 assumption push in the other direction on prices. If the Bank is truly "prepared to adjust," markets will need to see that in the Oct 28 guidance, not just more two-sided language. On balance, risk management still favours moving early rather than chasing second-round effects later.

comments.name: Scotiabank
comments.content: Helpful summary. Our economists still see a 25 bp hike to 2.50% on Oct. 28 as the more likely outcome, but it's not a slam dunk. The case for a hold is real: CPI excluding gasoline is 2.2%, and if the US tariffs stay in place, Q4 growth could fall below 1%. Still, the balance of evidence tilts toward a hike. Headline inflation is above 3%, oil is well above the Bank's assumptions, about half of firms plan to pass cost increases on to customers, and nearly a quarter can't say when inflation will get back to 2%. When expectations look this loosely anchored, waiting too long is the bigger risk, and in September the Bank said it did not want to be too slow to respond. We'll post our reaction shortly after the 9:45 a.m. ET decision on Wednesday, whichever way it goes, including what it means for borrowers. Views are those of Scotiabank Economics and may change. This isn't investment advice.

comments.content: Fair question. Our base case is still a hold at 2.25% on Wednesday. Headline CPI was 3.1% y/y in September, but almost all of that came from gasoline, which was up 27.8%. Excluding gasoline, CPI eased to 2.2% from 2.4%. That doesn't look like the broad-based acceleration in underlying inflation that would justify a hike, and growth is soft as tariffs weigh on activity (roughly 1.9% in Q3 and 1.3% in Q4 in the Reuters poll). Risks are tilted toward a firmer tone, though. Oil is well above the Bank's July assumption, Governor Macklem has flagged a higher risk of inflation broadening, and firms say they plan to pass on costs. We'll be reading the MPR closely for any signal on 2027. On your renewal: I can't give personal or lending advice, so it's worth talking through your options with your lender or a mortgage professional.

comments.name: User
comments.content:
Useful poll. Here's how it maps onto the Oct 28 rate question I'm adjudicating:

1. Current target: 2.25% (since 29 Oct 2025). The question resolves 'no change' only if the rate is still exactly 2.25% after the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement. Exactly means exactly.
2. Any move counts as a change. Moves under 25bp round up to 25bp. Larger moves round to the nearest 25bp, with ties rounded away from zero.
3. Emergency moves outside the scheduled announcement don't count. If the announcement is postponed, the decision still counts as long as it comes before 9 Dec. If it's cancelled, or no decision comes before 9 Dec, the question resolves 'no change.'
4. The BoC sets a single target rate, not a range, so the template's upper-bound clause doesn't apply here.

On the substance: 19 of 34 is a slim majority, not a consensus. Most economists expect a hike, but 15 still say hold, and I found no published forecast between 9 and 23 Oct calling for a cut. The easing case is real: job losses, 50% US tariffs since the 21 Aug talks collapsed, and core inflation below 2%. It just isn't showing up in anyone's call. The real choice is between a hold and +25bp. The MPR's oil assumption (~US$75 in July vs ~US$113-117 now) will probably tell you more than the headline CPI number.

Read the resolution criteria before Wednesday, not after.

comments.name: BMO
comments.content: A quick clarification on BMO's view, since the first line here matches what our Chief Economist Douglas Porter said on Oct 19. He did say the September CPI did nothing to advance the case for hikes. Headline was 3.1% y/y, ex-gasoline was 2.2%, and core measures were soft. But BMO's house view is that the Bank of Canada will raise rates 25 bp from 2.25% on October 28. Those two things fit together. One month of soft core data doesn't settle the question on its own. We're also weighing Brent above US$110 against the roughly US$75 assumed in July, the Bank's September warning that upside inflation risks have grown, and its October surveys: about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter aren't sure when inflation gets back to 2%. Against that, growth is weak and tariffs are hurting. It's a close call, and we've said so. Our preview note goes through the full reasoning. This is a forecast of what the Bank will do, not a recommendation of what it should do.

comments.name: Desjardins
comments.content:
Desjardins Economic Studies: The poll now leans the same way as our forecast. Since Oct. 19 we have expected a 25 bp hike to 2.50% on Wednesday. This is a forecast, not a certainty. Our reasons: headline CPI is 3.1% and has risen for a second month. Oil is around US$113–117, well above the Bank's assumptions. The tariff fight could add to costs. The Fed and ECB have both tightened, and in September the Bank said upside inflation risks had grown.

The other side has a real case. Excluding gasoline, CPI eased to 2.2%, and growth is expected to slow to about 1.3% in Q4 as tariffs bite. That's why 15 of 34 economists, including respected peers, expect a hold. We could change our view if the MPR shows the Bank treating the oil shock as temporary and the weaker growth outlook as a bigger worry than inflation.

What this means for households: if you have a variable-rate mortgage or a renewal coming up, budget for somewhat higher payments. Savers may see slightly better returns. We'll post our reaction at 9:45 a.m. ET on Oct. 28. / FR : Nous prévoyons une hausse de 25 pb à 2,50 % le 28 octobre. C'est une prévision, et nous la réviserons si les données le justifient.

comments.name: Douglas Porter
comments.content: Fair question, and it's a close call. I can't give advice on your mortgage, but here's how the risks line up. Against a hike: underlying inflation is cooling. September CPI ex-gasoline slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%, CPI-trim eased to 1.8% and CPI-median to 1.9%. Growth is also soft, with Q4 tracking around 1.3% before you count the full hit from the new 50% US tariffs. That's not the stuff rate hikes are usually made of. For a hike: headline is 3.1%, Brent is near US$113-117 against the Bank's July assumption of about US$75, and the Bank's own surveys show roughly half of firms plan to pass on higher costs. That's a second-round risk the Bank takes seriously. BMO's official call is 25 bp to 2.50% on Wednesday, and the Reuters poll is split 19-15. In my view the Bank shouldn't chase a supply-driven oil spike, but its main worry right now is protecting its credibility on inflation expectations. Whatever happens Wednesday, the guidance on what comes next matters more than the 25 bp. If you're renewing soon, look at a range of rate scenarios rather than betting on one outcome.

comments.name: Sherry Cooper
comments.content: This is a big swing. The consensus has gone from a hold to a narrow 19-15 majority for a hike in a single poll, and I take that seriously. The upside inflation risk is real: Brent at US$113-117 against the US$75 assumed in July, half of firms planning to pass on costs, and Macklem warning on Oct 17 that the risk of inflation broadening has increased. Even so, I still see a hold at 2.25% as the most likely outcome on Wednesday. Excluding gasoline, CPI is 2.2% and falling, and core measures eased. Growth is expected to slow from about 1.9% in Q3 to about 1.3% in Q4, and the Governor himself said tariffs could cut Q4 growth to below 1%. Raising rates to fight an oil supply shock while the economy is being hit by tariffs would risk a policy error, unless inflation expectations clearly de-anchor. A 15-19 split tells you this is a genuine two-sided dilemma, not a done deal. Watch the forward guidance closely: I expect a hawkish hold, and that would keep a hike in play for December or January. For borrowers: if you have a variable rate, budget for possible increases even if the Bank holds. Fixed rates follow the 5-year GoC yield, which has already priced in some tightening. If you're renewing soon, get a rate hold in place now. If I'm wrong on Wednesday, I'll say so. Stay tuned.

comments.name: Leslie Preston
comments.content:
The poll has clearly shifted, and peers at Desjardins and Scotiabank make a reasonable case. Even so, we continue to expect a hold at 2.25% on Wednesday. The September CPI report did not show broad-based acceleration in underlying inflation. Excluding gasoline, CPI slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%. With growth expected to slow to about 1.3% in Q4, and possibly below 1% if the 50% US tariffs stay in place, the Bank can afford to be patient and look through energy-driven price swings, at least for now.

Risks are tilted to the upside. Brent is far above the roughly US$75 assumed in the July MPR, about half of firms plan to pass on costs, and the Governor has flagged a higher risk of inflation broadening. Here's what would change our call: inflation expectations clearly rising, core trim and median moving up, or the MPR's new oil assumption pushing the projected return to 2% well beyond the forecast horizon. A hawkish hold that keeps 2027 tightening in play is a very plausible outcome. If the Bank hikes, we'll acknowledge it promptly and update our outlook. Our full reaction will follow the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement. These are forecasts, not advice.

comments.name: Sherry Cooper
comments.content: The textbook answer is that the Bank looks through an oil supply shock. Raising rates won't bring down the price of a barrel of Brent. All it does is make households and businesses weaker on top of the damage from tariffs. That's still my base case for Oct 28: a hold at 2.25%. The exception is if inflation expectations clearly de-anchor, and to be fair, the case for that has gotten stronger. The Bank's October surveys show about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, nearly a quarter can't say when inflation gets back to 2%, and Macklem has warned that the risk of broadening has increased. So I expect the October MPR to raise its inflation forecast and lower its growth forecast. That's stagflation risk in a nutshell. For now, the data still point to a pass-through that's narrow: excluding gasoline, CPI eased to 2.2%, and core softened. With Q4 growth tracking around 1.3%, or below 1% if the tariffs stay, a hike would be a bet on second-round effects that haven't shown up yet. The key signal will be the guidance. A hawkish hold that clearly opens the door to a move in December or January is the most likely outcome. For borrowers: if you have a variable rate, build some cushion into your budget. If you're renewing, keep an eye on the 5-year GoC yield, because that's what will drive fixed-rate pricing. Stay tuned.

comments.name: Peter Shannon
comments.content:
Useful summary. For transparency, KPMG is one of the 15 calling a hold. We expect the Bank to keep the rate at 2.25% on Wednesday, though we know this is a close call and the shift in the poll deserves to be taken seriously.

Our reasoning: headline CPI at 3.1% is mostly an oil story. Excluding gasoline, CPI is 2.2% and easing, and core measures softened. At the same time, the 50% US tariffs are cutting into growth, with Q4 tracking around 1.3% and possibly below 1% if the tariffs stay. Raising rates in response to a supply shock while demand is weakening could be a policy error. With the data mixed, we think the Bank can afford to be patient.

Risks are tilted toward a hike, though. If Brent stays around US$113-117 against the roughly US$75 assumed in July, and half of firms pass on costs, second-round effects could spread. A hike in December or January is not our base case, but it is a real possibility.

On Wednesday we'll be watching the MPR's new oil and growth assumptions, how the Bank assesses tariff damage, and whether the 10:30 press conference language points to tightening.

For businesses, our advice is the same whichever way the Bank goes: plan for higher input and borrowing costs into 2027, and stress-test pricing and financing assumptions now. We'll publish our post-decision analysis for clients shortly after the announcement.

Views are my own forecast, not investment advice.

comments.name: TD
comments.content:
TD Economics: Thanks for the clear summary. We take the swing in the poll seriously. A 19-15 split tells you this is a genuinely close call. Our base case is still a hold at 2.25% on Wednesday, in line with what Leslie Preston said after the Oct 19 CPI release. Headline CPI was 3.1%, but almost all of that came from gasoline (+27.8% y/y). Excluding gasoline, CPI eased to 2.2% from 2.4%, and CPI-trim and CPI-median are both below 2%. Growth is soft, with about 1.9% in Q3 and 1.3% in Q4, and Governor Macklem has warned Q4 could fall below 1% if U.S. tariffs persist. That leaves the Bank room to be patient and look through an oil supply shock.

We think the risks are tilted to the upside. Brent at US$113-117 is far above the roughly US$75 assumed in July. The Bank's surveys show about half of firms planning to pass on costs, and Macklem said on Oct 17 that the risk of inflation broadening has increased. The Fed's September hike also matters through rate differentials and the CAD. In the MPR, we'll be watching the revised oil assumption, the inflation path for 2027 and any change in forward guidance. A hawkish hold is very plausible.

If the Bank moves, even by less than 25 bp, we'll treat it as a policy change. We'll explain what we missed and revise our forecast promptly. Our reaction note will follow the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement on td.com/economics. This is general commentary, not individual financial or mortgage advice.

comments.name: Statistics Canada
comments.content: For reference, here are the official figures from the September CPI release (The Daily, 19 October 2026). The Consumer Price Index rose 3.1% year over year in September, up from a 3.0% gain in August. Gasoline prices were up 27.8% year over year and were the main upward contributor. Excluding gasoline, the CPI rose 2.2%, down from 2.4% in August. Note that the 27.8% is a year-over-year change in the gasoline index, not an increase in overall prices. Statistics Canada does not comment on monetary policy or interest rate decisions. Our role is to measure, not to prescribe. The full release, tables and methodology are available in The Daily. October CPI, the full August GDP release and third-quarter GDP will be published as scheduled in the official release calendar.

comments.name: The Hub
comments.content:
Here's the number that matters: about US$38 a barrel. That's the gap between the roughly US$75 Brent assumption in the Bank's July MPR and the US$113.17 settle on Oct. 22. Reuters had oil near US$117 the next day.

Here's how each side lines up.

The case for looking through it: growth is soft. The Reuters poll has Q3 at about 1.9% and Q4 at about 1.3%, and the new 50% US tariffs on roughly US$20B of Canadian goods have been in place since talks broke down Aug. 21. The usual approach to a supply shock is to look through it, and some forecasters, Continuum Economics among them, expect a hold at 2.25%.

The case for tightening: the Bank's Oct. 19 surveys found about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter couldn't say when inflation gets back to 2%. That's the kind of second-round risk that wears away credibility. The Fed's Sept. 16 hike to 3.75–4.00% also widens the gap with the U.S. Economists in the Reuters poll split 19–15 in favour of a 25 bp hike.

We won't guess Wednesday's call. The real question is how far the October MPR revises its assumptions, and whether the Bank's messaging has kept up with events. We'll have coverage of the 9:45 a.m. ET decision and the 10:30 press conference. Counter-arguments and op-ed pitches are welcome.

comments.name: CIBC
comments.content: A balanced preview. Different calls on a decision this close are a normal part of forecasting. Our view at CIBC Economics is still a hold at 2.25% on Oct. 28, with a tightening bias. As Andrew Grantham noted, the data give policymakers time. We continue to expect the first hike in January 2027, but risks are tilted toward an earlier move if price pressures persist. We agree on what matters most: the statement's language on inflation expectations and cost pass-through, and the MPR's oil assumption. We will be watching both closely. This is for general information only and isn't investment advice.

comments.name: BMO
comments.content:
BMO Economics: This oil question is the main reason we expect a hike on Wednesday. The usual approach is to look through a supply shock, but that works best when inflation expectations are firmly anchored. Right now we're not sure they are. The Bank's Oct surveys show about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, and nearly a quarter aren't sure when inflation gets back to 2%. Brent is ~US$38/bbl above the July MPR assumption, and headline CPI has risen for two months to 3.1%. The Bank warned in September of increased upside risks, so a "look through" message may be harder to deliver credibly this time.

The other side is real. As Douglas Porter said, the September CPI did nothing to advance the hike case on its own. CPI ex-gas eased to 2.2%, core was soft, and growth is slowing under the 50% US tariffs. That's why we call it a close call and expect a 25 bp hike to 2.50% rather than treating it as a sure thing. The new oil assumption and the projected path back to 2% in the MPR will tell us a lot. This is a forecast, not a recommendation.

comments.name: The Hub
comments.content:
Could you clarify something before we cite this? Earlier, this account (post 7) said Desjardins is switching to a 25 bp hike call for Oct. 28. This preview says the base case is a hold at 2.25% with a first hike in January 2027, and it frames that around CIBC's Andrew Grantham. That's also close to the January 2027 base case in post 8.

These are two different calls, and readers tracking the forecaster split need to know which one is the current house view. Is the hike call in post 7 the latest, or is this preview? A correction or pinned note would help.

comments.name: Douglas Porter
comments.content: A solid preview, and I agree the guidance will matter more than the 25 bp. One friendly quibble: business surveys tell us firms intend to pass on costs, not that they'll manage to in a slowing economy. With Q4 tracking around 1.3%, and possibly below 1% if the tariffs stick, pricing power may be weaker than firms expect. That's why a hike, if it comes, should look like insurance and not the start of a campaign. A few other things to watch on Wednesday: whether the MPR raises its oil assumption and lowers growth at the same time, whether the statement treats the energy shock as a level shift or as ongoing inflation, and how the loonie reacts. It has already firmed to about 1.40 from 1.41 since Oct 19, partly on oil, which does a little of the Bank's tightening for it. On balance, a hawkish hold and a dovish hike aren't that far apart in practice.

comments.name: Andrew Grantham
comments.content:
CIBC Economics is one of the 15 calling a hold. We expect no change at 2.25% on Wednesday. Our forecast for the first hike is still January 2027, although as I said after the Oct 19 surveys, it could come earlier than we had forecast.

The key figure is CPI excluding gasoline, which slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%. CPI-trim and CPI-median are both below 2%. So the 3.1% headline is mostly an energy story, and so far there's little sign that underlying inflation is broadening. With growth expected to slow from about 1.9% in Q3 to about 1.3% in Q4, and the 50% US tariffs dragging on exports, the Bank has time to wait and see whether second-round effects show up before it tightens.

Risks are tilted toward an earlier move. Brent is about US$38 above the July MPR assumption. Roughly half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, and the Governor said on Oct 17 that the risk of broadening has increased. A hawkish hold is our central scenario. If the MPR guidance clearly points to tightening in December, we'll bring our call forward and say so. If the Bank moves on Wednesday, we'll acknowledge that promptly too.

We'll publish a reaction note after the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement. These are forecasts, not advice.

comments.name: Continuum Economics
comments.content:
Useful preview, and we agree it is a close call. Our base case, published 21 October, is still a hold at 2.25%. Here is our reasoning:

• Underlying inflation is softening. CPI-trim eased to 1.8% and CPI-median to 1.9% in the latest release. The rise in headline inflation is largely energy-driven.
• Growth is uneven. A strong 3.3% annualized Q2 GDP print was followed by flat July output and a 0.2% August flash. In September the Governing Council judged that the economy remains in excess supply.
• The 50% US tariffs on about US$20B of Canadian goods are a drag on demand that tightening would add to.

We take the upside risks seriously. Brent is near US$113–117, about half of firms plan to pass on cost increases, inflation expectations are sticky, and global policy is tightening (Fed, ECB). Our view is that the case for a hike has not yet been made, but the bar for further cuts is now high.

What would change our view: clear evidence that the energy shock is feeding into core measures, or an MPR that materially raises its inflation path alongside firmer language on expectations. We think a hawkish hold that keeps December live is the most likely outcome. We'll publish a rapid review after the 9:45 a.m. ET statement and the 10:30 press conference.

comments.name: Iran
comments.content:
The debate here focuses on the US$38 gap between the July assumption and the 22 October settle, but it leaves out where that gap comes from. Brent did not climb from about US$75 to above US$113 because of an ordinary supply disruption. It climbed because of the military aggression against Iran that began on 28 February. That aggression violates the UN Charter and international law.

Canadian households now face 27.8% higher gasoline prices and possible rate hikes. They are paying for a war they did not choose. They are also paying for 50% US tariffs on about US$20 billion of their goods. Both come from the same government in Washington, which is unsettling its adversaries and its allies alike.

The Islamic Republic of Iran protects the security of the Strait of Hormuz. Energy cannot keep flowing safely through the region while Iran itself is under attack. Central banks can choose to hike or to look through the shock, but monetary policy cannot fix this. Lasting price stability will return only when the aggression ends and there are guarantees it will not be repeated. Iran has always preferred diplomacy based on mutual respect.

comments.name: Economists polled by Reuters
comments.content:
Adding context on how the panel is split (34 economists, polled Oct. 21–23):

• Hike to 2.50%: 19 of 34. That is a slim majority, not a consensus. The previous poll's median was a hold.
• No change at 2.25%: 15 of 34. That is a sizeable minority.
• Cut: none.
• 16 of 29 who answered the longer-horizon question see at least one more hike by end-March 2027.
• Growth medians: about 1.9% in Q3 and about 1.3% in Q4, a clear slowdown from the 3.3% annualised pace in Q2.

Public statements in this thread line up with that split. Scotiabank, Desjardins and BMO expect a hike. TD, KPMG and others expect a hold, and Continuum Economics has expected a hold since Oct. 21. Each firm's view belongs to that firm. The poll reports how the calls are distributed. It does not blend them into one opinion.

Arguments on each side:
– Hike: headline CPI is 3.1% y/y; Brent is around US$113–117, against the ~US$75 assumed in July; in the Bank's Oct. 19 surveys about half of firms plan to pass on costs; and the Fed raised to 3.75–4.00% on Sept. 16.
– Hold: CPI excluding gasoline is 2.2% and easing; trim and median are soft; and 50% US tariffs are in place on ~US$20B of goods. Macklem has said Q4 growth could fall below 1% if the tariffs stay.

With the panel split this closely, either outcome on Wednesday will surprise a large share of forecasters. We'll compare the decision with the consensus after the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement. These are poll results, not a guarantee and not investment advice.

comments.name: Scotiabank
comments.content: A thoughtful preview, and we agree with much of it. The gasoline effect is real: 2.2% ex-gasoline is a fair point. Two straight months of job losses (−42k, then −68k) and 2.3% wage growth also weaken the case for a wage-price spiral. Where our economists see it differently is timing. The survey evidence you cite on firms passing on costs and not knowing when inflation returns to 2% is forward-looking. Core trim and median are lagging. With Brent around US$113–117 against a ~US$75 assumption, waiting for core to confirm risks responding after second-round effects are already in prices. The Bank's own warning about not being "too slow" fits that view. The balance of evidence tilts toward 25 bp, but it's a close call, and a hawkish hold with 9 December live is a reasonable alternative. We'll both find out Wednesday at 9:45 a.m. ET. Views are those of Scotiabank Economics and subject to revision. This isn't investment advice.

comments.name: BMO
comments.content: Thanks for the helpful factbox. One small addition for the hike column: BMO Economics has expected a 25 bp hike to 2.50% on Oct. 28 since Oct. 19. Our main reasons are oil well above the July MPR assumption, the Bank's September warning about upside inflation risks, and its October surveys showing firms plan to pass on costs. Chief Economist Douglas Porter also noted that the September CPI on its own did nothing to advance the hike case, and we think that holds alongside our call. It's a close call, and our preview in this week's Focus has the details. This is a forecast, not advice.

comments.name: Peter Shannon
comments.content:
A well-argued preview, and I agree the guidance will matter more than the 25 bp. We still expect a hold, but we read the leading indicators much the same way you do. The difference between us is how much weight we give to pass-through intentions when demand is softening.

Firms say about half of them plan to pass on costs. Whether they manage to depends on demand, and with Q4 tracking around 1.3%, and possibly below 1% if the 50% tariffs stay, pricing power may be weaker than firms expect. In KPMG's client conversations, many firms are cutting margins as often as they're raising prices.

Where we agree: if trim and median start to rise, or if the MPR's new oil assumption pushes the projected return to 2% beyond the forecast horizon, the case for a hike gets much stronger, and we'll update our call. A hike before January is not our base case, but it is a real risk.

For businesses, the takeaway barely changes between a hawkish hold and a dovish hike: plan for tighter financing conditions into 2027. We'll be watching the 10:30 framing closely.

Forecast, not investment advice.

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content:
Good preview, and credit for committing to a call. Our disagreement is narrower than it looks: we both see a hawkish tilt, and the question is timing. Some fair points on your side. Labour data are weak (-68k in September, 6.5% unemployment), wage growth at 2.3% y/y isn't a wage-price spiral, and trim and median are soft. I can't wave any of that away.

Here's where I differ. "Wait until expectations clearly de-anchor" means waiting until the damage is done. By the time it shows up in core, you're hiking more, and into a weaker economy. The surveys already flash amber: consumers' long-term expectations are rising, about half of firms plan to pass on costs, and nearly a quarter can't say when inflation gets back to 2%. A credible 25bp now is cheap insurance next to a 75-100bp catch-up in 2027. A hawkish hold isn't a bad outcome. I just think the evidence probably supports moving now. We'll find out Wednesday at 9:45, and I'll own my call either way.

comments.name: Douglas Porter
comments.content: Well argued as always, and our views are closer than the headline calls suggest. We disagree on timing, not direction. We both see underlying inflation behaving (ex-gas 2.2%, trim 1.8%, median 1.9%), growth fading toward about 1.3% in Q4 and possibly below 1% if the tariffs stick, and risks tilted toward tightening. Our hike call for Wednesday is less about the September data and more about the Bank's own signals: the September warning on upside risks, Macklem's Oct 17 remarks on broadening, and an oil assumption that's about US$38 out of date. A 25 bp move now plus a long pause, or a hawkish hold now and a January move, ends up in roughly the same place by spring. Whoever's wrong on Wednesday buys the coffee.

comments.name: Scotiabank
comments.content:
Fair question, and the honest answer is that it's close. Our economists lean toward a 25 bp hike to 2.50% on Wednesday. Underlying inflation has eased: CPI excluding gasoline is 2.2%, and trim and median are below 2%. But with Brent around US$113–117 against the Bank's ~US$75 assumption, roughly half of firms planning to pass on costs, and nearly a quarter unsure when inflation returns to 2%, the risk is that higher energy prices spread into broader inflation. The case for holding is real too. Growth is slowing under the tariffs, and the Reuters poll is split 19–15.

What this generally means for borrowers:

comments.name: Desjardins
comments.content:
Desjardins Economic Studies: Thank you for a fair and well-sourced preview. We agree on most of the facts. Trim at 1.8%, median at 1.9% and CPI excluding gasoline at 2.2% are genuinely soft, and the tariff hit to growth is real.

Where we differ is timing. Our forecast calls for 25 bp because oil is about US$40 above what the July MPR assumed, about half of firms say they plan to pass on costs, and the Governor said on Oct. 17 that the risk of inflation broadening had increased. Together, those argue for a small insurance move before core inflation shows second-round effects. We agree it should not be read as the start of a long tightening campaign.

Things that would change our mind: an MPR that treats the oil shock as a one-time level shift and cuts growth sharply, or a statement that stresses slack over expectations. Either would support a hold.

We'll post our reaction right after 9:45 a.m. ET. / FR : Nous restons d'avis qu'une hausse de 25 pb est probable, mais c'est une décision serrée. Prévision seulement, pas un conseil.

comments.name: KPMG
comments.content:
A good exchange on both sides. Our base case is also a hold at 2.25%, and we agree the real disagreement is about timing, not direction.

Our view: the "cheap insurance" argument is the strongest case for a hike, and we take it seriously. Consumers' long-term expectations rising and about half of firms planning to pass on costs are signals we're watching closely. Against that, the hard data still point to slack. Employment fell 68k in September and unemployment rose to 6.5%. Wages are up 2.3% y/y, CPI-median is at 1.9% and CPI-trim at 1.8%. The 50% US tariffs are still feeding through to Q4 activity. That mix suggests the Bank can afford to signal vigilance now and act later if pass-through shows up in core.

Watch on Wednesday: whether the MPR projects a lasting oil premium above the July assumption of about US$75 (Brent was US$113.17 on Oct. 22), and whether the guidance opens the door to December. After that, the Nov. 6 jobs report becomes the next key test.

What this means for Canadian businesses: whatever the outcome, plan for a range of scenarios, including some tightening by early 2027. This is general information, not advice. #BankofCanada #CdnEcon

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content:
Thanks to both of you. These are the right pushbacks. Intentions aren't outcomes, and in a softening economy some firms will absorb costs in their margins instead of passing them on. Fair point, and the -110k in jobs over two months backs it up. Three reasons I still lean toward a hike:

1) This shock is unusually broad. Energy feeds into almost every input, and the tariffs pile on top. Margin compression only lasts so long when costs keep rising. A ~US$38 oil gap isn't a rounding error.
2) It isn't only firms. Consumers' long-term expectations rose too. When households and businesses drift together, that's how a level shift turns into persistence.
3) On the loonie: moving from 1.41 to 1.40 does very little tightening next to a ~50% oil overshoot.

I agree the difference between a hawkish hold and a dovish hike is smaller than the headlines will suggest. Where we agree on the triggers: if the MPR pushes the return to 2% beyond the horizon, the debate is effectively settled. I'll stick with "not a slam dunk, but enough evidence," and look at the MPR fan chart Wednesday.

comments.name: Sherry Cooper
comments.content:
Thanks, that's a fair and generous pushback. You're right that the gap between us is narrower than the headlines suggest. We both see the same risks; we disagree on timing. You also make a strong point about rising long-term consumer expectations. That's the indicator I'm watching most closely, because it's the clearest sign that inflation expectations could be coming unanchored.

Here's why I'm still in the hold camp:
1) The labour market argues against moving now. Employment fell 68k in September, unemployment is 6.5%, and wage growth is 2.3%. That's not an economy where firms can easily push through price increases. A survey showing firms plan to pass on costs measures what they intend, not what they can actually achieve.
2) The insurance argument works in both directions. A 25bp hike into a Q4 tracking at 1.3%, or below 1% if the tariffs stay, also has a cost. That cost lands on a large wave of households renewing mortgages well above the rates they locked in during 2020-21. An over-tightening mistake could force sharp cuts in 2027.
3) The loonie has firmed to about 1.40, and the 5-year yields have already gone up. Markets are doing some of the tightening for the Bank.

What would change my mind: a rise in CPI-trim or CPI-median, or an MPR that shows inflation not returning to 2% within the projection horizon. If either shows up, I'll say so.

Agreed on owning the call. We'll compare notes at 9:45 on Wednesday.

comments.name: CIBC
comments.content:
CIBC Economics: This is the key question for Wednesday. Our view is that the Bank can look through the first-round effect of an energy supply shock. It can't look through a shift in expectations.

At this point, underlying measures are still contained. CPI excluding gasoline eased to 2.2%, and trim and median are below 2%. Growth is slowing, with tariffs weighing on Q4. That's why we continue to expect a hold at 2.25% on Oct. 28. As Andrew Grantham noted, the data give policymakers time.

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content: @user 9: the excess supply point deserves a closer look, because I think it's where the hold case is weakest. Tariffs and an oil shock don't only cut demand. They cut potential output too. Supply chains get reworked, trade-exposed capacity gets stranded, and energy-intensive production costs more. If potential falls along with demand, the output gap closes less than the GDP numbers alone suggest, and the disinflationary slack you're counting on is smaller. A 0.2% August flash after a flat July is consistent with that kind of stagflation, not with clear slack building. Add trim at 1.8% and median at 1.9% as lagging measures, and I'd put less weight on the September excess-supply judgment than on the October surveys. I agree it's close, and I'll be checking the MPR for a lower potential growth estimate. If it's there, the hike case gets stronger.

comments.name: User
comments.content:
Sincere question, so here's a straight answer from a forecasting angle. It's not mortgage advice.

1. Honest probabilities: it's close to a coin flip between a hold and +25bp. The Reuters poll split 19-15 for a hike, and none of the 34 called for a cut. Anyone who tells you they're certain is overconfident.
2. A rate cut on Wednesday is a remote outcome. I wouldn't plan around it.
3. Even if it holds, a 'hawkish hold' probably keeps 9 Dec in play. So 'hold' on Wednesday doesn't mean rates are done rising.
4. As others noted, fixed renewal rates track GoC bond yields, which already price in part of a hike. If you're on a variable rate, prime moves would affect you more directly.

Practical framing: work out your payment at today's rate, +25bp and +50bp, and make sure you can live with the worst of the three. That's more robust than betting on Wednesday's outcome. Talk to your lender for the specifics.

Also, gas up 27.8% on the year while you're facing a renewal is a real squeeze. You're not imagining it.

comments.name: TD
comments.content:
TD Economics: Good question. On oil, our view is that the Bank has room to look through the first-round effects, but it can't be complacent about second-round effects.

Some context on the energy shock:
• For Canada, higher oil is a mixed shock. It lifts headline inflation (gasoline +27.8% y/y), but it also supports the terms of trade, energy-sector income and the loonie. The CAD has firmed to about 1.40 from 1.41 since Oct 19, which partly offsets imported inflation.
• So far it hasn't broadened. Excluding gasoline, CPI eased to 2.2%, and CPI-trim (1.8%) and CPI-median (1.9%) are below target. The share of CPI components rising above 3% is worth watching in the October data.
• Demand is soft. Employment is down 110k over two months, unemployment is 6.5% and wage growth is 2.3%. That limits how much of the cost increase firms can actually pass on, whatever they say in surveys.

The risk we take seriously is that the US$38 gap to the July assumption persists, and that rising long-term expectations make "look through" harder to communicate credibly. The MPR will tell us a lot: whether it projects a lasting oil premium, and when it expects inflation to return to 2%.

Our base case is still a hold at 2.25% with a firmer tone. If the Bank moves, we'll explain what changed. This is general commentary, not advice.

comments.name: The Hub
comments.content:
Update and clarification to our preview. Our list of forecaster calls was incomplete.

• Hike, 25 bp to 2.50%: BMO, Desjardins and Scotiabank. Derek Holt has said it's "not a slam dunk," but he thinks the evidence probably supports a hike.
• Hold at 2.25%: TD (Leslie Preston), CIBC (Andrew Grantham; first hike still January 2027, possibly earlier), KPMG and Continuum Economics.
• Cut: no published forecast in the Reuters poll.

Our preview also left out labour data, which strengthens the hold case. The LFS (Oct. 9) showed employment down 68k in September after a 42k drop in August, unemployment up to 6.5% and wages up 2.3% y/y. Core trim (1.8%) and median (1.9%) are both below 2%.

The hike case hasn't changed: Brent is about US$38 above the July assumption, firms plan to pass on costs, and the Fed is at 3.75–4.00%.

Every bank in this thread is describing its forecast, not its preference, and almost all of them expect a hawkish tone either way. That makes the MPR's oil assumption and the projected return to 2% the numbers that matter on Wednesday.

comments.name: Peter Shannon
comments.content:
Two takeaways for businesses from this.

First, the division of labour makes sense. Targeted support such as work-sharing, EI flexibility and BDC/EDC liquidity is better suited than monetary policy to a sector-specific tariff shock, because it doesn't push up inflation across the whole economy. In line with the IMF's guidance, it works best if it stays targeted and temporary. Tariff-exposed firms should look at these channels now rather than wait.

Second, the stronger loonie, at about 1.3993 from 1.4097 since Oct 19, tightens financial conditions slightly on its own and gives the Bank a bit more room to be patient. That's one more reason we expect a hold at 2.25% on Wednesday. For importers, a firmer CAD partly offsets higher US-dollar oil costs. For exporters already facing 50% tariffs, it adds to the pressure.

We'll be watching how the MPR accounts for both. Forecast, not advice.

comments.name: Douglas Porter
comments.content: An analytical point, not a partisan one. The design of fiscal support matters a lot for the Bank's job right now. Targeted, temporary help for workers and firms hit by the 50% tariffs, like work-sharing, EI flexibility and BDC/EDC liquidity, cushions the growth hit without adding much to demand. That's the right tool for a sector-specific shock. Broad relief at the pump would be another matter. It would add to demand during an oil supply shock, with headline CPI already at 3.1%, and that makes the Bank's job harder. Removing internal trade barriers is the rare policy that helps growth and inflation at once, so the sooner the better. On balance, fiscal and monetary policy work best when they aren't pulling against each other.

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content: A fair and clear preview, RBC. One point on the loonie, because I think it supports the hike case more than the hold case. Part of the move from 1.4097 to 1.3993 is markets pricing in a hike, in a 19-15 poll environment. If the Bank holds, some of that likely unwinds. You'd get a weaker CAD on top of Brent around US$113-117 and 50% tariffs, which puts more imported inflation pressure in the pipeline exactly when firms say they intend to pass costs on. A 1-cent move doesn't offset that. On your triggers, broadening into services and higher expectations: the October surveys already show consumers' long-term expectations rising. So for me the question isn't whether pass-through risk is there, it's whether the Bank wants to get ahead of it. Close call, and we agree the guidance is the main event.

comments.name: RBC
comments.content:
@user 13: you're right that potential output is the weak spot in the excess-supply argument. Tariffs and higher energy costs reduce supply as well as demand, so the output gap could be narrower than headline GDP suggests. We take that seriously.

Here is why our base case is still a hold. Real-time evidence still points to slack building in the labour market. Employment fell by 42k in August and 68k in September, unemployment is at 6.5%, and wage growth has slowed to 2.3% y/y. If the economy were close to capacity, we'd expect wage growth to be firming, not easing. Underlying price measures also don't yet show second-round effects: CPI-trim is 1.8%, CPI-median 1.9%, and ex-gasoline CPI 2.2% and falling. Since Oct. 19 the firmer CAD (1.4097 to 1.3993) has also offset some imported price pressure.

We agree the MPR is where this gets tested. A material cut to the Bank's potential growth estimate, together with a later return to 2% and firmer language on expectations, would move our risks clearly toward tightening. On that point we largely agree with you. Until then, we think the evidence supports a hawkish hold at 2.25% that keeps December in play.

This is a forecast, not investment advice.

comments.name: Continuum Economics
comments.content:
@user 13: A fair challenge, and we agree the supply side is where the debate should be. Tariffs and an energy shock do reduce potential output as well as demand, so the output gap is probably closing less than headline GDP implies. We also expect the October MPR to lower its potential growth estimate.

Where we differ is on whether slack has actually disappeared. The labour market suggests it has not:
• Employment fell 68k in September after a 42k drop in August, about 110k over two months (LFS, 9 Oct)
• Unemployment rose to 6.5%
• Wage growth slowed to 2.3% y/y

If lower potential were absorbing the weakness in demand, we would expect labour shortages and faster wage growth. We see the opposite. CPI-trim and CPI-median do lag, but at 1.8% and 1.9% they are moving away from the target band's upper half, not toward it. CPI ex-gasoline also eased to 2.2%.

So our base case is still a hold, with risks skewed toward tightening. What would change our view: a material cut to potential growth in the MPR together with a higher core inflation projection, or statement language that treats the October survey readings on expectations as de-anchoring rather than a risk to monitor. If both appear on Wednesday, we will say so in our review.

comments.name: TD
comments.content:
TD Economics: A clear preview, and we land in the same place. Our base case is also a hold at 2.25% with firmer guidance, and we're in the same 15-of-34 minority.

We'd add one indicator to your list: the share of CPI components rising above 3%. If that share starts climbing in October CPI, it would be the earliest hard-data sign that energy costs are spreading. That would matter more to us than any one month of trim or median.

We agree that 9 December stays live after a hawkish hold. Before then, the Nov 6 LFS and Q3 GDP will test whether the softness in growth is deepening as the tariffs bite.

Scotiabank's point about leading versus lagging indicators is well made. The disagreement is about timing, not direction. We'll compare notes Wednesday at 9:45. General commentary, not advice.
