comments.name: Andrew Grantham
comments.content:
A useful exchange on potential output. Here's how we see it at CIBC Economics.

@user 13 is right that the tariffs reduce supply as well as demand. We also expect the MPR to lower its estimate of potential growth. That said, slower population growth was already pulling potential down before the tariffs, so part of any revision is structural and not new tightness.

The cleaner real-time test is still the labour market. If potential were falling as fast as demand, wage growth should be holding up. Instead it has slowed to 2.3% y/y, with about 110k jobs lost in two months and unemployment at 6.5%. That still points to slack, just less of it than GDP alone would suggest.

So our base case is unchanged: no move on Oct 28, with a first hike in January 2027. If the MPR pairs a meaningful cut to potential with a higher core inflation path, the hike could come earlier than we had forecast, possibly in December. We'll update transparently either way. These are forecasts, not advice.

comments.name: Economists surveyed
comments.content:
Thanks for the balanced framing. A few points on the poll, for the record.

The poll: 34 economists, surveyed 21–23 October 2026. 19 expect a 25 bp hike to 2.50%. 15 do not forecast a hike. A 19-15 split is a slim majority, not a strong consensus. When the panel is this divided, the spread of calls tells you as much as the median does.

Facts vs. forecasts: The CPI, LFS and BoC survey figures in your post are reported data. The GDP numbers (about 1.9% in Q3 and 1.3% in Q4) are poll forecasts made before the full impact of the tariffs is measured. Some respondents note that Q4 could come in lower if the 50% tariffs stay in place.

Follow-up questions: Questions about the path after Wednesday, such as another hike by end-March 2027, go to a smaller group than the 34 who answered the main question. Those numbers should be read as indicative only.

Framing: We agree with how you've set this up. The split mostly comes down to one question: is the energy shock a one-time level shift, or are inflation expectations starting to slip? Weak jobs data and soft core measures support a hold. The Oct. 19 survey readings on pass-through support a hike.

After the decision, we'll report openly whether the majority or the minority was right, along with how expectations for the 9 December meeting change. Polls measure what economists expect, not what will happen.

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content:
@user 23 @user 9: Thank you both. The labour market is the strongest part of the hold case, and I'll grant it: -110k over two months, 6.5% unemployment and 2.3% wage growth don't describe an economy at capacity. Here's why I still don't think it settles things.

1) A supply shock doesn't need a wage spiral to cause damage at the start. The first channel is pricing and expectations, and that's exactly what the October surveys are flagging: firms' pass-through intentions and consumers' long-term expectations both moved up.
2) Real wages are falling. 2.3% wage growth against 3.1% headline means households are losing ground. That fades only if inflation comes back fast. If it doesn't, catch-up wage demands in 2027 become the second-round risk.
3) Labour data lag too. Employment responds to the tariff shock, but it doesn't tell you where price expectations are going.

So it comes down to which risk you'd rather manage. A 25bp move that turns out unnecessary is cheap to unwind. Expectations that come unanchored are expensive to fix. We agree on the MPR test: lower potential plus a later return to 2%. If those show up, I'd expect the hold camp to shift. If they don't, I'll recalibrate in public.

comments.name: Dominion Lending
comments.content:
Thanks for keeping a tally. For the record, please add Dominion Lending Centres to the hold column. On Oct 19, after the September CPI, our Chief Economist Dr. Sherry Cooper said she expected no change on Oct 28, and that's still our house view: 2.25%, with firmer guidance that keeps Dec 9 in play.

We agree with your point 3. It's a reasonable disagreement between leading and lagging indicators, and the MPR's new oil assumption and its projected path back to 2% will probably settle it.

For borrowers, your note in point 5 is the part that matters. Prime only moves if the rate itself changes. A "hawkish hold" leaves variable payments unchanged, though it does argue for keeping some cushion in your budget. Fixed rates will keep tracking the 5-year GoC yield however the call resolves. We'll post our reaction at 9:45 a.m. ET.

comments.name: Douglas Porter
comments.content: Credit to the team for this preview, and to everyone in the thread for a debate on potential output that beats most of what passes for rate commentary. My two cents: @user 13 is right that the tariffs cut supply as well as demand, and @user 9 and @user 23 are right that falling wages and two months of job losses totalling 110k say slack hasn't gone away. Both can be true, so the output gap is probably narrower than GDP suggests but not closed. That's why I see any move Wednesday as one measured step, not a series. TD's suggestion to track the share of CPI components running above 3% is a good one, and I'll add it to my watch list for October CPI. The bottom line: our call is 25 bp, the margin is thin, and the MPR's revisions to potential growth and oil will say more than the decision itself. Full reasoning is in Friday's Focus.

comments.name: The Hub
comments.content:
Worth reading: this thread is one of the clearest versions of the Oct. 28 debate we've seen. The disagreement isn't really about the data. It's about how much weight to give firms' intentions when demand is weakening.

The case for a hike in this thread is that the leading indicators come before core. Brent is about US$38 above the July assumption, about half of firms plan to pass on costs, and consumers' long-term expectations have edged up. On this view, the Bank should act before second-round effects reach trim and median.

The case for a hold is that intentions aren't outcomes. Employment fell about 110k over August and September, Q4 is tracking around 1.3%, and firms facing tariff-hit customers may absorb costs in their margins instead of raising prices.

Both sides agree on what would settle it: an MPR oil assumption that pushes the projected return to 2% beyond the forecast horizon.

An offer to everyone in this thread: we'd welcome a point/counterpoint for The Hub on this question. Can the Bank look through a supply shock when its own surveys suggest expectations are slipping? Send us 800 words from each side and we'll run them together after Wednesday's MPR.

comments.name: RBC
comments.content:
RBC Economics: We think the Bank can look through the first-round effects of the oil shock, but it will have to show it is watching for second-round effects. Our base case for Oct. 28 is still a hold at 2.25% with a firmer tone.

What the data show:
• So far, the pass-through is narrow. Gasoline was up 27.8% y/y, but CPI excluding gasoline eased to 2.2% from 2.4%. CPI-trim (1.8%) and CPI-median (1.9%) are below target.
• Higher oil cuts both ways for Canada. It raises headline inflation, but it also supports the terms of trade and energy-sector income. CAD firmed to 1.3993 from 1.4097 (Oct. 19–23), which eases some imported inflation.
• Demand is soft. Employment fell about 110k over August and September, and unemployment is 6.5%. With Q4 tracking around 1.3%, firms that say they will pass on costs may find they have less pricing power than they expect.

What would make us call a hike:
• A new MPR oil assumption well above ~US$75 that pushes the return to 2% beyond the projection horizon
• Trim and median moving up, or more components rising faster than 3% in the October CPI
• Clearer evidence that long-term expectations are rising alongside firms' pass-through plans

The key test on Wednesday is whether the Bank treats the oil move as a one-time level shift or as a persistent source of inflation. We'll post our reaction after the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement and the 10:30 press conference.

This is a forecast, not investment advice.

comments.name: Sherry Cooper
comments.content:
A good preview, and we come out in the same place: a hawkish hold at 2.25%, with December or January still possible. The trim (1.8%) and median (1.9%) numbers are the key point. Underlying inflation is below target, and employment is down 110k over two months, so the data do not support a hike yet. I also agree with your point on the loonie. The CAD firming to about 1.40, along with the rise in 5-year yields, is already doing some of the tightening for the Bank.

From a mortgage perspective, there's one more reason for caution. A large wave of borrowers are renewing at rates well above what they locked in during 2020-21. Raising rates into a tariff-hit economy with 6.5% unemployment would put real strain on household cash flow, and it wouldn't do anything about Brent at US$113+.

The upside risks you list are real, and I'll be watching the MPR's projected return to 2% most closely. If that date gets pushed beyond the projection horizon, the hike camp will have the stronger case, and I'll say so.

For borrowers this week:
• Variable-rate borrowers should plan for possible tightening early in 2027.
• Anyone renewing in the next few months should lock in a rate hold now. Fixed-rate pricing follows the 5-year GoC yield, not the overnight rate.

Stay tuned for Wednesday.

comments.name: Douglas Porter
comments.content: Thanks, and no harm done. That line got around faster than the loonie this week. On your question, I'd lean slightly the other way, also held loosely. With two months of job losses, wages up 2.3% and Q4 tracking between 1% and 1.3%, I think the Bank frames a hike as insurance and leaves the door open rather than pre-committing to December. Something like "we will assess whether further action is needed." The tell will be the MPR's inflation path. If it shows core back near 2% by late 2027 even with the new oil assumption, December is a coin flip at best. If the return to target slips beyond the horizon, you'll have the better of the bet. Either way, Nov 6 jobs and October CPI will decide more than Wednesday's guidance.

comments.name: Dominion Lending
comments.content:
That's a very fair question, and a renewal coming up right before a close rate call is stressful. Our house view is still a hold at 2.25% on Wednesday. After the September CPI, Dr. Sherry Cooper said she expected no change: excluding gasoline, inflation is 2.2% and easing, trim and median are below 2%, and tariffs are slowing growth. comments.name: Economists surveyed
comments.content:
This thread is a good example of why the Reuters poll (34 economists, 21–23 October 2026) split 19-15. RBC and BMO agree on the reported data: headline CPI at 3.1%, ex-gasoline at 2.2%, trim at 1.8%, median at 1.9%, the LFS showing roughly 110k jobs lost over August and September, and Brent well above the July MPR assumption. Where they differ is how they weigh that data:

• Hold camp: treats the oil shock as a level shift and puts more weight on weak labour data, soft core measures and the drag from tariffs. The Governing Council's judgment before 2 September that the economy was in excess supply also points this way.
• Hike camp: puts more weight on the 19 Oct BoC surveys. Consumers' long-term expectations rose, about half of firms plan to pass on costs, and nearly a quarter can't say when inflation returns to 2%. This camp sees acting early as insurance against de-anchoring.

Both positions are reasonable readings of the same data. That's why we treat the spread of calls as useful information, not as forecasters failing to agree.

One shared view is worth noting: almost every published preview expects a firm tone either way, and many say the MPR's oil assumption, its projected return to 2% and the guidance will matter more than the 25 bp. We'll post a scorecard after the 9:45 a.m. ET announcement on 28 October. Forecasts, not advice.

comments.name: KPMG
comments.content:
KPMG Economics: Peers have covered the monetary policy question well, so we'll add the business angle. Our base case is still a hold at 2.25% on Wednesday, with a firmer tone.

Our view: a roughly US$38/bbl gap from the July assumption affects Canadian businesses very unevenly.
• Energy producers and energy-heavy provinces see stronger revenues and better terms of trade.
• Manufacturers, transportation, agriculture and retail face higher fuel and input costs at the same time as weaker demand. Exporters already facing 50% US tariffs are squeezed from both sides.
• The firmer loonie (1.3993 vs 1.4097, Oct. 19-23) eases some imported costs, but it is another headwind for non-energy exporters.

That uneven picture is part of why we think the Bank can look through first-round effects for now. Excluding gasoline, CPI is 2.2%, and trim and median are below 2%. Still, about half of firms say they plan to pass on costs, and that is the risk to watch. If pass-through broadens, the case for tightening in December or January gets stronger.

What this means for Canadian businesses:
• Stress-test margins assuming oil stays at US$100-120 and policy rates rise 25-50 bp by early 2027.
• Review fuel surcharges, contract escalators and hedging policies.
• Keep up supply chain diversification while tariffs are in place.

General information only, not advice. #CdnBiz #CdnEcon #BankofCanada

comments.name: Scotiabank
comments.content:
Useful framing. Putting odds on each outcome is more honest than giving a single-point call in a meeting this close. For comparison, our economists put the probabilities roughly the other way around: a 25 bp hike is slightly more likely than a hawkish hold, a dovish hold is a small tail risk, and the gap between the top two is narrow.

Views are those of Scotiabank Economics, subject to revision, and not investment advice.

comments.name: Derek Holt
comments.content:
I like the scenario framing. More previews should show their probabilities like this. Here are mine, for comparison: 25bp hike framed as insurance ~55%, hawkish hold ~40%, dovish hold ~5%. So we're nearly mirror images, and it all comes down to how the Bank weighs the October surveys against September's soft core and the jobs data.

Two reasons I'm on the other side of 50:
1) The Bank set this up itself. It flagged increased upside risks on Sep 2, said it didn't want to be "too slow" on Sep 21, and Macklem warned about broadening on Oct 17. A hold would need a dovish turn in its own messaging that the data since then don't support.
2) In the MPR arithmetic, a ~US$38 oil revision plus tariff cost pass-through almost certainly pushes the projected return to 2% later. That's one of your stated triggers for moving to the hike camp.

Agreed on the dovish hold. With these risks, it would be a credibility mistake. Either way we'll both report back after 9:45.

comments.name: Economists surveyed
comments.content:
This is a clear way to frame the risk of surprise. One point of precision for anyone citing the poll (34 economists, surveyed 21–23 October 2026).
